summary: Defines the Format and DelSp parameters for the text/plain media type. Trailing spaces mark flowed lines, so text can rewrap nicely while still looking like ordinary text in older programs. A canonical quote indicator marks quoted lines. It supersedes RFC 2646 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Emails can look broken when a program breaks lines in the wrong places. This adds invisible hints so the text re-flows nicely on any screen, but old programs still show it fine.

questions: how does flowed email text work
subtitle: How a trailing space lets plain-text email reflow to any screen while still reading as ordinary text.

tldr.problem: Plain-text email gets hard-wrapped at a fixed width, so quoted replies end up with ragged, confusing lines and messages look bad on narrow screens.
tldr.mechanism: The Format=Flowed and DelSp parameters on Text/Plain mark a soft line break with a trailing space before the CRLF, and mark quoted lines with leading > characters. Aware programs rejoin and rewrap the text, and older programs just show plain text.
tldr.outcome: It supersedes RFC 2646 and adds DelSp so the scheme works for languages that rarely use ASCII spaces.

today: RFC 3676 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2646, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem With Fixed Plain Text
sections.content:
Text/Plain is the lowest common denominator of Internet email. Lines are at most 998 characters, by convention usually no more than 78, and a CRLF ends each line. It is normally shown as preformatted text, so a line longer than the window either wraps or forces a horizontal scroll bar. The RFC calls this style fixed text. Many modern programs instead use flowed text, where line breaks are soft and only a CRLF ends a paragraph.

Two problems follow. When messages are quoted in replies and forwards, each line grows until it is arbitrarily hard wrapped, which the RFC calls embarrassing line wrap. It also gets worse on small devices with narrow displays. Attempts to use new media types such as Text/Enriched and Text/HTML lacked backward compatibility and drew hostile user reactions. Some programs treat unknown TEXT subtypes as attachments.

What was needed is a format that is in all significant ways Text/Plain, yet tells the receiver which lines are quoted and which form a logical paragraph that may be rewrapped.
sections.eli5: If you copy a sentence onto short strips of paper, it looks silly on a wider page. Flowed text lets the page glue the strips back together and cut them to fit.

sections.title: The Format and DelSp Parameters
sections.content:
Two MIME parameters are added to Text/Plain. Format takes Fixed or Flowed, and DelSp takes Yes or No. Names and values are not case sensitive. If Format is missing or not recognized, Fixed is assumed. If DelSp is missing or not recognized, No is assumed. The use of DelSp without Format=Flowed is undefined. The RFC describes an on-the-wire format, not local file storage, and the content-transfer-encoding does not matter to flowed processing.

The trick is that a flowed line ends in a space. A line that ends in a space is flowed, otherwise it is fixed. A series of one or more flowed lines followed by one fixed line is a paragraph, which may be wrapped or unwrapped. An empty line (just a CRLF) is a fixed line. If DelSp is yes, the trailing space is logically deleted when the lines are joined. Otherwise it stays as a normal space between words.

Receivers SHOULD tolerate improperly built messages: a flowed line ends the paragraph if the next line has a different quote depth or is a signature separator, and the end of the body also ends a paragraph.
sections.eli5: An invisible space at the end of a line means "this sentence keeps going on the next line." A line with no such space means "I am finished." A second setting says whether to throw that invisible space away when joining.

sections.title: Generating Flowed Text
sections.content:
A generating program SHOULD keep every line, including trailing spaces and any stuffing space, to 78 characters or fewer, not counting the CRLF. The limit is 78 rather than 79 or 80 because the last column is often reserved for a line-wrap indicator. As suggested values, it could wrap paragraphs at 72 or fewer characters. Soft breaks go at natural places such as between words. A word longer than 78 characters (but under 998) is sent as is.

There are two ways to insert a soft break. The older technique from RFC 2646 inserts a CRLF after an existing space, and then DelSp SHOULD be used and, if used, MUST be no. The newer technique inserts a new space and a CRLF (SP CRLF), works for languages where spaces are rare, and requires DelSp to be present and set to yes. A program MAY use either method within each body part.

Other generation rules:

  • It MUST NOT place soft breaks so that any line becomes a signature separator.
  • It SHOULD trim spaces before user-inserted hard line breaks.
  • Quoted-Printable SHOULD NOT be used unless absolutely necessary, because it hurts the raw readability that is the point of the format.
  • Hand-aligned text such as tables, art and source code SHOULD be sent as fixed lines.
sections.eli5: When writing the message, the sender chops long paragraphs into short lines and leaves the invisible space on each cut. Tables and drawings are not chopped at all, so they stay neat.

sections.title: Quoting, Space-Stuffing and Signatures
sections.content:
The quote indicator is one or more > characters at the start of a line, and their count is the quote depth. Quote marks are counted and removed first, before any other test. All lines of a paragraph MUST be unquoted, or all quoted at the same depth. So the line before any change in depth MUST NOT be flowed. A receiver that finds a flowed line there SHOULD apply the quote-depth-wins rule and end the paragraph. To reformat quoted text, a receiver de-quotes, reformats, then re-quotes with the same number of marks.

Space-stuffing adds one extra space at the start of a line that needs protection. A generating program MUST stuff unquoted lines starting with > and any line starting with a space or From . This protects against systems that rewrite From to >From in transit. A receiver removes one leading space after counting quote marks and before checking for flowed.

The Usenet signature separator, dash dash space (-- ), ends in a space but is neither flowed nor fixed, and it is sent as is. A paragraph MUST NOT end with one.

The RFC gives ABNF for all of this. A flowed body is any number of paragraphs, fixed lines and signature separators, and a paragraph is one or more flowed lines followed by a fixed line.
sections.eli5: Every extra arrow at the start of a line means one more layer of "somebody said that." A leading extra space is a little bumper that keeps odd-looking lines from being mistaken for something else.

sections.title: Compatibility and Failure Modes
sections.content:
Because flowed lines are all but indistinguishable from fixed lines, software that does not know the format shows them as ordinary Text/Plain, with only some trailing spaces added. Unreversed space-stuffing may leave a leading space on rare lines. Messages with DelSp=yes read by a program that knows Format=Flowed but not DelSp will keep an extra space after soft breaks, so for languages where spaces are common a sender MAY always use DelSp=no.

Some systems alter trailing whitespace. Stripping it turns flowed lines into fixed lines, which is no worse than not using the format. Adding it may cause malformed display or replies. The RFC considers using one or two trailing spaces to counter this, and decides that, given how scarce such systems are, it is not worth the added complexity.

The RFC also warns that rewrapping can change the text between composition and sending and between receiving and display. Signing or encrypting a message needs care, and cryptographic processing should use the on-the-wire text. Because OpenPGP cleartext signatures ignore trailing whitespace, trailing spaces could be added in transit unnoticed, so OpenPGP with flowed messages is strongly discouraged and OpenPGP-MIME is recommended.
sections.eli5: An old program just sees ordinary text with a few extra invisible spaces, so nothing breaks. The only real trouble comes if something along the way messes with those invisible spaces.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2646
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the changes from RFC 2646. The main change is the new DelSp parameter for languages and coded character sets in which the space is less common or not used. The RFC also notes that the Internationalization section warns that line wrapping and quoting may not suit right-to-left scripts such as Arabic and Hebrew, where fixed text with quoted-printable may be better.

The 79 or 80 character limits became 78 to match RFC 2822, and the limit now explicitly includes trailing white space and stuffing. Some SHOULDs became MUSTs (space-stuffing and quoted paragraphs), the ABNF was rewritten to remove most ambiguity, and text was added saying that the end of the body ends a paragraph. The RFC explains that the DelSp mechanism was chosen even though it was first rejected as too much of a kludge, because it gives the most interoperability among old and new clients.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition. It adds one new setting so the trick also works in languages that do not put spaces between words.

items.title: Starts with >
items.text: Quoted. The marks are counted for the quote depth and removed first.

items.title: Starts with a space
items.text: Space-stuffed. That one leading space is removed.

items.title: Ends in a space
items.text: Flowed, so it joins the next line (except the signature separator).
